analysis.one_liner: Lets generic drug makers sue brand manufacturers that withhold drug samples needed to develop cheaper copies.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan CREATES Act of 2016 was introduced with sponsors from both parties and received a Senate subcommittee hearing, but it never received a vote in the Senate before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug makers control a small supply of their drugs, and some use that control to keep generic companies from getting the samples they need to test and win approval for cheaper copies. This bill would let a generic or biosimilar developer sue a brand manufacturer that refuses to sell samples on market terms or refuses to share safety protocols, and courts could order the samples delivered and award the generic developer fees and damages. The bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay brand-name drug prices when a cheap generic copy is delayed, along with the taxpayers who fund federal health programs, and the generic and biosimilar companies that would gain a legal tool to break the delay tactics the bill's findings describe.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high brand-name drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a civil action letting a generic developer sue a brand manufacturer that declines to sell it 'sufficient quantities' of the drug on commercially reasonable, market-based terms, with a court order to provide the samples as the remedy.

The bill's own findings state that some brand manufacturers have used FDA-required safety programs (REMS) and self-imposed distribution restrictions as a reason not to sell samples to generic developers, delaying cheaper competition, and that FDA has received many inquiries from generics blocked from getting samples; the FDA and the FTC chairwoman testified to these concerns.

For drugs with a REMS safety protocol that generics must join, a developer denied entry for 120 days could sue to be let into a single shared system, with court orders and deterrence payments capped at the brand's revenue during the delay.
Drugs already in shortage are carved out of the bill, so the new lawsuits cannot pull supply away from a medication that is already scarce.
The bill includes a liability shield: the brand manufacturer is not liable for injuries caused by a generic developer's mishandling of the product during testing.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the ability to stretch out their exclusive pricing through sample refusals and safety-protocol stalling, and would face court orders, attorney fees, and deterrence payments up to their revenue on the drug during the delay.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new federal cause of action with deterrence-style damages capped at the brand's revenue during the delay, which critics of later versions of the bill warned would invite litigation and give generic companies leverage to force pay-for-delay style settlements rather than develop their products.

Sample provision and shared safety protocols exist for safety reasons under the FDA's REMS program, and opponents argued that forcing sales outside a brand's chosen distribution system, even with the bill's FDA authorization step and liability shield, loosens safety controls around drugs that carry special risks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and large for patients: getting a generic to market typically cuts that drug's price sharply, and the bill targets a specific, documented delay tactic rather than rewriting drug regulation wholesale. The trade-offs are real but narrow: a new litigation channel with capped but substantial damages, and a modest loosening of how tightly high-risk drugs are distributed during testing, with an FDA authorization step and a liability shield designed to address the safety objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got a subcommittee hearing, and then sat there until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 without ever coming to a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the bill on June 14, 2016, with Senator Grassley (R-IA), Senator Klobuchar (D-MN), and Senator Lee (R-UT) as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee.

It attracted 11 cosponsors, 6 of 54 Senate Republicans and 5 of 44 Senate Democrats, and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Competition Policy and Consumer Rights held a hearing on June 21, 2016.
That was the last action on the bill; no committee vote was ever recorded and it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
A nearly identical CREATES Act was reintroduced in later congresses and eventually became law in 2019, indicating the delay tactic the bill targeted remained live policy ground.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: their ability to use sample refusals and safety-protocol stalling to delay generic competition continued unchallenged, and patients kept paying brand prices for drugs whose cheap copies could have arrived sooner.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CREATES Act of 2016 in the Senate and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 11 of 98 senators
for.role: Cosponsors (6 of 54 Senate Republicans, 5 of 44 Senate Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill across party lines.

for.name: FDA and FTC
for.role: Federal agencies overseeing drug approval and competition
for.what_they_did: FDA's drug center director and the FTC chairwoman testified that REMS and closed distribution systems were being used to block generic developers from getting samples and delay generic competition.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of brand drugs and biologics (led in Washington by PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and its later versions, arguing it created a litigation vehicle and weakened REMS safety controls.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democrat-Republican pairing from the start: Leahy, Grassley, Klobuchar, and Lee sponsored it together, and its 11 cosponsors split 6 Republicans and 5 Democrats.

industries.note: The bill strips away their ability to delay generic and biosimilar competition by refusing to sell samples or stalling shared safety protocols, ending what the bill's findings describe as revenue earned from extra years of brand-only pricing. Their interest in keeping that tactic runs directly against patients paying brand prices.
They gain a tailored cause of action to obtain the samples and protocol access they need for FDA approval, making them the vehicle for bringing lower-priced copies to patients sooner.
